clean_source_blocks.text: Miles Wang, an OpenAI researcher whose work includes using AI to accelerate scientific and biological discovery, is leaving the ChatGPT maker to launch a new startup focused on developing AI models for drug discovery, according to four people with knowledge of his plans. Several other OpenAI researchers are expected to join the new company. Wang is in talks to raise about $200 million at a $2 billion valuation, two of the people said. Lightspeed is in discussions to lead the funding round, according to sources. Talks are ongoing, the deal may not be final and details could change. ---
The funding discussions point to investor interest in applying AI to make breakthroughs in life sciences.

OpenAI published results on June 17, 2026, from a three-month collaboration with Polish chemistry startup Molecule.one that marks the first publicly documented instance of a frontier AI model acting as a near-autonomous agent in a real wet-lab chemistry workflow — one that produced a validated, independently confirmed improvement to a reaction medicinal chemists have struggled with for decades.

The result involves Chan–Lam coupling, a copper-catalyzed method chemists use to form carbon–nitrogen bonds that are ubiquitous in medicines. Coupling primary sulfonamides — a pharmacophore found in over 91 FDA-approved drugs spanning oncology, antimicrobials, and cardiology — with boronic acids has historically returned low yields, making the reaction a known bottleneck in early-stage drug discovery. Working with Molecule.one, OpenAI's GPT-5.4 identified an unexpected fix: the stable radical TEMPO, used as a mild oxidant, substantially improved yields across a wide range of substrate combinations.

The result came out of a near-autonomous experimental loop that ran 10,080 reactions — more than a bench chemist running three experiments a day would complete in a decade.

Chan–Lam coupling was independently discovered in 1998 by three research groups simultaneously and rapidly became valuable in medicinal chemistry because it uses inexpensive copper catalysts and tolerates air and moisture — unlike competing palladium-based methods. However, its mechanism has an inherent vulnerability with electron-withdrawing substrates.

The reaction runs through a copper catalytic cycle: copper(II) acetate reacts with the boronic acid partner to form a copper–aryl intermediate, which then reacts with the amine to form the product and releases copper(I). For the reaction to turn over and form more product, that copper(I) must be reoxidized back to copper(II). Under standard conditions, ambient oxygen from air does this reoxidation. But for primary sulfonamides — whose electron-withdrawing sulfonyl group weakens the nitrogen's nucleophilicity — this copper reoxidation step is sluggish, competing reactions consume the boronic acid through protodeboronation, and yields stay low.

TEMPO (2,2,6,6-tetramethylpiperidin-1-oxyl), a commercially available stable organic radical used for decades as an oxidant in alcohol chemistry, can accelerate exactly this reoxidation step.
